blocks.x: Epidemic Sound announced a partnership with Overwolf and MyPart to launch a new Stream mode in Songhunt, the Overwolf in-game app that gives PC gamers a personalized, adaptive music experience across more than 1,500 PC games.

Songhunt uses MyPart's multimodal AI to interpret gameplay continuously and select music from Epidemic Sound's catalog that matches what is happening on screen, shifting from quiet exploration to fast-paced combat.

For streamers on Twitch and YouTube, Epidemic Sound's 100% IP-owned catalog removes the risk of muted VODs, copyright claims and takedowns. "Songhunt removes that trade-off," said Rasmus Thofte, SVP B2B at Epidemic Sound.
On the latest episode of Las Culturistas, Kelly Clarkson said a lot of good can come from AI: "Controversial? I don't care: I love AI. ... I'm into it artistically, too. I have fun with it."
She called most opinions on AI music too "black-and-white": "I think it's welcome to the table ... but I don't think they should be competing with humans."
"When you see AI artists competing on a chart with humans, I have an issue," she said. "I think there should be a separate chart ... We can't lose human."
In August, Billboard reaffirmed its commitment to transparently note when an AI-generated song enters its charts, as Luminate announced plans to label AI-created content.

Shoegaze outfit SLEEP CLUB's latest single "Weight Of Ease", from their upcoming debut album "Dweller", has seemingly been incorrectly flagged by Spotify for AI usage. The band's entire catalog had previously been flagged before Spotify resolved it.

"For the 2nd time in two releases, our newest single 'Weight of Ease' has been flagged by Spotify's AI driven internal system as 'ineligible for recommendation'," said Matt Jones, noting algorithmic support makes up roughly 50-70% of an average artist's streams. It took roughly 5 weeks to restore the catalog.

"It's ironic that this album, which is about the intrusion of AI into every aspect of our lives, keeps getting flagged by AI systems incorrectly," he added. The band later said the first flag stemmed from the word "sleep" in their name; Spotify has not explained the current one.

AWS walks through deploying a music production pipeline on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, managed EC2 infrastructure that adds multi-day sessions, GPUs, persistent volumes and colocation of multiple agents.

blocks.cap: The three-agent pipeline (Compose, Deliver, Screen) sharing one GPU instance and session

blocks.x: A composition agent turns a producer's request into a brief with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and renders audio with the open-source ACE-Step model on the instance's NVIDIA L4 — 20 seconds of 48 kHz stereo in about 9 seconds. A delivery agent measures the .wav and applies an EQ, compression and limiting chain; a compliance agent re-measures it and screens it against the studio's back catalog, asking for a replacement if it flags a match.
Invoked with the same session ID, the agents share one instance and filesystem, and sessions can persist for up to 14 days.

blocks.cap: Melofty Axom Max audio processor

blocks.x: Startup brand Melofty has released the Axom Max audio processor. It packs new modeling technology, a 'real-time' tracking guitar synth, an AI assistant that builds rigs, and possible NAM-A2 support. Gearnews says it does everything short of selling merch at the venue.
It's notable that 'Guitar' was dropped from the product name. That signals it's aimed at a wider range of musicians, not just guitarists.

Each amp and pedal capture made with Melofty's proprietary MFIM (Multidimensional Fusion Inverse Modeling) technology contains up to 9,856 parameter points. Players who want to dive straight in can choose from more than 400 amps, more than 130 effects, and more than 200 IRs.

blocks.cap: The AI assistant used via smartphone app

blocks.x: If there's too much to choose from, the smartphone AI assistant can handle it. Type or speak a request like '80s British Stadium Rock' or '70s Psychedelic,' and it produces a signal chain linking virtual pedals, amps, and IRs, matched as closely as possible to the desired tone.

There's also DeepSynth, a synth for guitar and bass. It tracks pitch in real time without a MIDI pickup, and includes over 50 synth sounds plus instrument modeling that makes a guitar sound like other instruments (a feature similar to the Boss VG-800).

blocks.cap: DeepSynth instrument modeling screen

blocks.x: Up to 19 effects can be applied to a single preset. By routing two inputs separately, guitar and bass can also be played at the same time on one unit. There are 504 preset slots, with up to 6 scenes per preset.

It also includes a stereo looper that records up to 60 minutes, plus vocal effects like tuning, harmonizer, and reverb. Control centers on a 7-inch touchscreen, with 8 footswitches, 4 knobs, and an expression pedal. Connected to a computer, it becomes an 8-in/8-out audio interface.

It is priced at 1,299 euros. Thomann is taking orders, with shipping expected in 2-3 weeks. Right out of the gate it's priced to compete with Tonex, Helix Stadium, and Quad Cortex, which Gearnews called a bold move, adding that it is waiting for the first reviews.

blocks.cap: Spotify and Meta's AI agent Muse

blocks.x: Spotify has detailed how it works inside Meta's personal AI agent Muse. Linking the two services lets users talk with Muse to play music, save songs, and build Spotify playlists.

Spotify has been one of Muse's connectors since the agent launched on September 8. At the time, Meta's chief AI officer Alexandr Wang listed it alongside Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable and Plaid. Spotify posted the integration details on its blog on September 23, the same day Meta put Muse at the center of its product strategy in the Menlo Park Connect keynote.

Spotify describes it this way: "The agent can play music on Spotify, save songs to your library, build playlists, and help find books or podcasts. It's all done through conversation." The example given is a road trip: you can ask it to build a driving playlist suited to your destination and have it start playing the moment you leave. It can also resume a podcast you left off, or play a saved playlist through your kitchen speaker.
Muse can also create a 'Personal Podcast' that turns daily briefings, notes or ideas into audio and adds them to your Spotify library.

Muse runs on a dedicated virtual machine Meta calls the Muse Secure VM, powered by a model called Muse Spark. It first launched in the US on iOS, Android and muse.ai, followed by a Mac version on September 17 and a Canada launch the next day. The Spotify integration is also limited to the US and Canada for now. Meta says it checks with users first before sensitive actions like sending emails or making payments.

For Spotify, this extends a strategy of using other tech companies' AI assistants as distribution channels. The company said "Spotify is already available on more than 2,000 devices, from cars, TVs and speakers to ChatGPT and Claude." It added recommendation features to ChatGPT in October 2025, and struck a similar deal with Anthropic's Claude this past April.
Meanwhile, Amazon has blocked Muse from shopping on its site, citing data security and disclosure concerns. Spotify described the integration as "just the beginning."

blocks.cap: San Jose Sharks pull a goal song accused of being AI-generated

blocks.x: The NHL's San Jose Sharks are changing their goal song. The new track arrives on October 1. The previous goal song, 'Power Bite,' lasted exactly one season. Allegations that it was AI-made sparked a strong backlash from fans.

The backlash grew louder after online sleuths pointed out the song was likely made with Suno, the AI music platform that is as controversial as it is popular. The Sharks ultimately decided to drop the song.

Hockey teams typically have a dedicated song that plays when a goal is scored at their home arena. Since their inaugural season in 1993, the Sharks had used Gary Glitter's arena-rock staple 'Rock and Roll, Part 2.'

'Power Bite' was reportedly chosen by fans, but it drew criticism for sounding 'cheap.' Critics also accused the team of picking a bland, 'soulless' track to save on licensing fees for well-known arena hits.

The term 'AI slop' gained traction after online sleuths found that BVRNOUT appeared to have made the track with Suno. Fan frustration grew further when the team did not directly address the allegations.
And now the Sharks have ended the 'Power Bite' era. In a new video, defenseman Sam Dickonson switches off the speaker that played the song and announces, "The new goal song arrives on October 1."
Digital Music News predicted that the Sharks will not make their next goal song with AI.

blocks.cap: Sony Music Group joins ARIAM

blocks.x: Sony Music Group has joined ARIAM (Alliance for Responsible Innovation in the Arts & Media), an AI policy coalition. It is the first music company to do so. ARIAM launched in June 2026 with member companies from film, TV, journalism, publishing, education and technology.

The move was announced on September 23 by ARIAM president Victoria Furniss. Existing members include The Walt Disney Company, Fox Entertainment, ITV, BBC, Adobe, Condé Nast, Financial Times and The New York Times.

Sony Music Entertainment COO Kevin Kelleher said, "Generative AI is both a major opportunity and a challenge for artists and songwriters," adding, "We joined ARIAM to help shape how AI fits into the future across the creative industries." He added that Sony fully shares ARIAM's view that the only foundation is a healthy licensing environment in which responsible AI companies partner with rights holders first.
Furniss welcomed the move, saying, "The issues surrounding AI span the entire creative community, and music is an essential part of that conversation."

ARIAM says it aims to work with the content and technology industries to build legal and policy frameworks that are 'responsible by design,' going beyond copyright to protect consumers, especially children, and creators. It is headquartered in Los Angeles and led by Furniss, a former Netflix and Warner Bros. executive.
Music Ally quipped that ARIAM's self-description—"an outcomes-focused, solutions-oriented global coalition spanning the content industries"—must have gone through quite a few rounds of sign-off.

Sony Music Entertainment is the only major label that has not signed licensing deals with Suno or Udio. It filed a second lawsuit against Udio on July 20, and on September 18 sued Suno again alongside Universal Music Group.

blocks.cap: Fred again.. (Photo: Theo Batterham)

blocks.x: Fred again.. said he is opposed to using AI in music.

The British DJ and producer posted several Instagram Stories on September 25. The post revisited thoughts on AI that he had written in his phone's notes app a year earlier. "I've been thinking about this for a while, and the opposite of AI music might not be human music. It's making music."

"The process is the magic. Anyone lucky enough to have made music, or anything, has probably felt this in their own way for a long time. That's probably why I've never felt any urge to try AI. I put a lot of my identity into the process, and I've never felt that was a bad choice."
He also said the process of coming up with ideas and making music is a kind of 'meditation' for him. "Handing that process to a machine fundamentally conflicts with what I love about this work."

The post ended like this: "Clumsily but persistently rolling toward one idea. Trying endlessly, for hours, for years, to make something you wish existed. That's the greatest luck we get to have. There's a lot I worry AI might threaten, but never this."

Fred again..'s Instagram Story

blocks.x: Skrillex and Daft Punk's Thomas Bangalter have also recently voiced reservations about AI publicly.
Earlier this month, Fred again.. was named as a contributing artist on the GTA VI soundtrack, with the track 'Sexy Magic' featuring PinkPantheress, Etienne de Crécy, and CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso.

Music startup Thoughtful Things has launched a Kickstarter campaign for its first instrument, Engram. It's a sampler and groovebox that uses AI to mangle incoming sound, and even hallucinate sounds that were never there.

But it's not a boxed-up Suno. It's nothing like a device that spits out radio top-40 songs at the push of a button. It's built to make experimental, strange sounds and push AI audio models past their limits.

Engram doesn't connect to the internet. Instead, it runs a “small AI” inside the device itself. According to the Kickstarter page, the model was designed and trained in-house. Here's how the company explains it.
“We trained our audio models on open datasets containing only audio cleared for commercial use, such as CC-BY. We have never trained on non-commercial, pirated, or stolen data, and we never will.”

The firmware will also be open, letting anyone tinker with it or upload their own models. In the campaign video, founder Evan King asks for “piano” by voice, and Engram spits out a glitchy, hazy approximation of a piano.

King asks people to think of Engram as a “field recorder for latent space,” a machine for exploring AI hallucination and experimental sound design. Inspired by circuit bending, it can twist a small AI model until it breaks.

Thoughtful Things is offering only a limited number of Engram units on Kickstarter, starting at $675. The company hasn't disclosed the retail price, but the $675 backer price is listed as a 30% discount, suggesting it will likely land around $850 to $900.
ElevenLabs has released Studio 4.0, an agentic video editor built into ElevenCreative. It creates video, images, voice, music, and sound effects directly inside the project.

Describe the shot you need in text, and that shot lands on the timeline, placed alongside voiceover, music, and images. If you don't like it, you don't have to start over; you can just refine that one shot, and editing, captions, and export all happen in one place.

The timeline supports frame-level zoom and clip snapping, and moving clips doesn't throw off the sync. Captions are treated like any other clip: you can split a cue, merge two of them, or fix a mistranscribed word right away.
The AI co-editor, Studio Agent, drafts a cut from a single prompt. Users can take over editing at any point and hand it back to the agent again.

That doesn't mean AI is useless for audio work. Russ Hughes, founder of Production Expert, admits AI plays a big role in rescuing unusable audio and sorting hundreds of thousands of sound effects. Generative AI that fills in dropped sections during recording is useful too.

What he takes issue with is generative AI that produces music, writing, or images from a single prompt. The deeper he dug, he writes, the more he found that the technology is 'boring by design.' Models run on probability, guessing only the most likely answer a human might write, sing, or play.

Gated reverb is a good example. It came about when someone left the talkback mic on an SSL console switched on while working out a drum part. The location was the Stone Room at Townhouse Studios, and the talkback had a gate on it. Nobody was looking for that sound, but someone said 'that's not bad' and kept it, and it ended up on the record.

Generative AI is good at ruining things with hallucinations, but it can't create moments like this. When Hughes asked Suno for "music no one has ever heard," it produced three unremarkable pop songs. Asking for "something original" got the same result.

He draws a line against the argument that better algorithms will fix this. The structure itself, built to guess what comes next, is what produces predictable answers. Loosening the temperature value only produces garbage instead of magical accidents.

To the question of whether humans are also influenced by what they've seen and heard, he calls that a 'false equivalence.' Human creation comes from experience; generative AI comes from pattern. Suno can sing about loss but has never felt loss.
As a final experiment, Hughes played his wife the Suno output. She said she didn't like it, then, without being asked, asked back, "Is this AI?"

Last month's deal between Suno and BMG became a test that splits how artists really feel about AI. Mötley Crüe is on the okay side. Manager Allen Kovac said the band would “opt in if it's a paid deal,” adding that “AI promotes music, it doesn't dilute it.”

Not everyone is this optimistic. Suno touts a $5.4 billion valuation, 2 million paying users, and 100 million users who have made a song. The BMG deal includes an opt-in clause that artists choose themselves, but music attorney Dina LaPolt said “none of our clients would do that.” She praised BMG for choosing opt-in over opt-out.

Besides BMG, WMG and Believe have also partnered with Suno, which unveiled its v6 model on September 9. On September 18, UMG and Sony Music filed a new lawsuit adding 61,000 songs, calling v6 “fruit from the same poisoned tree.”

How each deal actually secures artist consent remains unclear. Attorney Harold Pappineau pointed out that, depending on contract terms, some artists may not be able to opt out. BMG's Celine Joshua drew a line, saying “this is not a blanket deal without consent.”

Attorney Ben McLane, who represents Afroman and others, called it “the way of the future” and said he would advise clients to take part. The real question is royalty splits, and none of the deal announcements spell out what songwriters and artists get.

Eric Greenspan, who represents Red Hot Chili Peppers, Dead & Company, and the E Street Band, advises always building an opt-out right into any deal. “Suno and Udio both keep rolling out new plans. It's the wild, wild West while artists, labels, and tech companies hunt for a business model.”

Composer Michael Whalen believes we've been asking the wrong questions about generative AI. More important than whether AI will replace musicians or whether Suno survives its lawsuits is the fact that the music industry is splitting in two.

One side is synthetic music, made fast, consumed fast, and swapped out just as quickly. The other is artist music, where identity, ownership, history, and fan relationships still matter most. Blue Dot Music founder Nicholas Gunn agrees. "We're entering an era where two kinds of music business coexist."

AI solved a scarcity problem the music industry never actually had. Music has always been abundant. What was scarce was attention, trust, cultural presence, and the relationship between artists and audiences. AI increased supply but failed to increase demand.

Synthetic music can still be a big business, in places with a clear use: playlists, games, fitness, meditation, in-store background audio. But that isn't an artist career. On the artist side, direct relationships with fans—websites, mailing lists, live shows, physical merchandise—matter more than ever.

Both worlds will likely remain on streaming platforms, increasingly distinguished by AI labeling. Whalen believes metadata will mark the difference before the day comes when no one can tell the difference at all.

The Suno lawsuits are where 'music AI 1.0' and '2.0' collide. Warner and BMG have signed licensing deals, and Suno itself said it would retire older models once next-generation ones arrive. The market is demanding licensing before any court has even ruled.

That could leave songs made with early models as 'stranded tracks.' They wouldn't become illegal, but once distributors, music supervisors, and catalog buyers start asking about provenance, moving them elsewhere gets harder. Whalen's conclusion is short: music that can travel is worth more than music that can't.

blocks.cap: Musixmatch founder and CEO Massimo 'Max' Ciociola

blocks.x: Call Musixmatch just a 'lyrics company' and Massimo 'Max' Ciociola might tilt his head. It's true the company built its name organizing lyrics in songs. Now it works with nearly 250,000 rights holders and is used by more than 80 million people worldwide. The lyrics scrolling beneath songs on Spotify, YouTube, Apple Music and Instagram belong to this company.

Collecting and monitoring lyrics in more than 250 languages has already turned it into a 'sophisticated royalty management company,' he says. 'We've evolved into a kind of fintech company. Our core business is processing royalties.' The next goal is a company that manages rights through multiple AI agents to protect rights holders and songwriters.

In October 2025, Musixmatch signed 'AI innovation' agreements with the three major publishers, securing a catalog of 15 million songs. This March, it launched Sentinel, a real-time copyright-detection service for UGC platforms. It flags even partial lyric infringement as a user types a prompt, with a verdict in under 100 milliseconds.

Its first major client is Suno. Suno confirmed in August that it had adopted Sentinel. When a Suno user tries to make music by entering lyrics from an existing song, Sentinel filters it out. Musixmatch has positioned itself as neutral infrastructure, selling to rights holders who want to protect their catalogs and AI companies that want to stay within the law. It also unveiled Music Lens, an AI 'music agent' that lets publishers analyze the meaning, mood and context of their catalogs.

The NMPA estimated that in 2024, lyrics licensing accounted for only 1% of publisher and songwriter income. Ciociola believes that figure badly undersells the potential of lyrics. 'In the language of AI, lyrics are becoming the LLM of the music industry. They're literally the language of music.' He says that within a few years, searches by song title will shift to prompts like 'make me a playlist of breakup songs,' with lyrics at the center of it.

On the rights holders' lawsuits against Anthropic and Suno, he said he is 'entirely on the side of IP owners.' He predicted Anthropic will settle with music rights holders, adding, 'It has to be fixed, and it will be.'

blocks.cap: Atomix VirtualDJ 2026

blocks.x: VirtualDJ 2026 has received its third and final update. AI features have grown again. Alongside Shoutouts, which lets users create their own voiceovers and lyrics, a feature that writes scripts from simple text descriptions has been added.

VirtualDJ 2026 was built from its first version with AI integration at its center. A Gearnews writer argues the new features add little to traditional mixing. But if you see mixing as the complete 'atomization' of music, it opens up entirely new, perhaps slightly unsettling possibilities. Atomix says it isn't chasing trends but adding AI features that are genuinely useful to DJs.

In the second update, which followed the December launch, AI automatically generated visuals that moved in sync with the beat. A fluid beatgrid and BPM stabilization feature also arrived then, along with improved AI lyric recognition.
The new Shoutouts feature lets users insert their own voiceovers and lyrics into a track as it plays. Custom drops, live edits and announcements are all handled without leaving the DJ software.

AI Scripting lets DJs build their own customizations and extensions inside the software without programming skills. Writing a prompt in plain language produces a script, letting users reshape controls and workflows their own way. Much as Ableton Live released extensions, other apps are likely to follow a similar path.
Compatibility with various DJ controllers has improved, and support for some streaming services, including Spotify, has expanded. VirtualDJ 2026 users again receive the update for free.

blocks.cap: ClassicalBot screenshot

blocks.x: Today brought an unusual cluster of interesting, creative uses of AI in music. After Engram, ClassicalBot is the next story in the news. It's a project started by Slovak developer Robert Druska.

He first built it to map classical concerts in his home country, then expanded it worldwide. He wrote on the site: "From the start, this project was an experiment in how far AI automation could go. Almost everything you see here — source discovery, extracting concert information, program analysis — is handled by AI in some way."

How it works is detailed in a blog post, which introduces concepts like a 'magic box' and a 'crawler factory.' Druska believes the technology he built can be used outside music too. "The idea of an automated crawler factory can be extended to any purpose. You could build a loop to scrape every restaurant menu in a city, online shop prices, job listings, every kind of event, or corporate data."

ClassicalBot, first introduced by the Bliss music library management blog, shows how much a single developer can build. Whether it turns into a business remains to be seen. Still, it's an interesting case that might push others to build something of their own.

Oliver Thor is shaking up sound. Together with the duo MIRA新伝統, he bends the tempo of Ableton Live and builds drum kits out of YouTube chaos trawled by AI. The founder of the Glazmo Network, Thor has spent years digging into the “mythology of sound,” and he has just released two tools that anyone who enjoys uncertainty and glitches should grab.
CDM first came to know Thor through Bastl Instruments. He went on to work as a producer and now lives in Athens, where he shares his sound design process on the Glazmo Network Discord.

blocks.cap: Agitator

blocks.x: Agitator, made by MIRA新伝統 and Thor, grabs hold of a project's entire tempo and shakes it. Feed it audio and it resets the whole project tempo, with slew controls for smoothing, rise, and fall. Just set a minimum and maximum value and drop it on a track. It works like Ableton's Envelope Follower, except the stock device can't touch tempo. It costs €3 (pay more if you like) and requires Ableton Live 12 or later plus Max for Live.

blocks.cap: GLAZMO_DREAM_PORT

blocks.x: GLAZMO_DREAM_PORT twists the black box of AI prompting. Generated Zen koan fragments become YouTube search terms, and the returned audio gets chopped up and loaded onto pads.

Hit the encryption button and it can flip into a glitchier, dreamier “corrupted” version. The plugin also generates provenance information so you can clear rights before release. It exchanges files with its host via drag and drop, and it's macOS-only, supporting VST3 for both Apple Silicon and Intel.

Michael Smith, a North Carolina man who admitted to using bots to play AI-generated songs billions of times and collect more than $8 million in royalties, has asked a federal judge to spare him prison time. According to Billboard, his lawyers want a sentence of probation.

His lawyers filed a sentencing memo at Manhattan federal court on September 22. They argue Smith's conduct caused only “a vanishingly small, unmeasurable loss” spread across millions of songwriters and artists. “The impact of one play of one artist's song on the market share of every other artist is a drop in the ocean, not a drop in a bucket. No artist or songwriter suffered any discernible harm from Mr. Smith's conduct.” The memo also claims 'major labels' did the same thing.

They asked the judge to weigh his lack of a criminal record, his history of good conduct, and the impact imprisonment would have on his family. “He made a serious mistake here, but that mistake does not define who he is.”

Smith pleaded guilty in March to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The maximum sentence is five years in prison. Federal sentencing guidelines call for 46 to 57 months, while the U.S. Probation Office's pre-sentence report recommended a shorter 24 months. Prosecutors have not yet filed a sentencing position. Under his plea agreement, Smith also agreed to forfeit more than $8 million. His sentencing, originally set for July 29, did not take place, and no new date appears in the public record.

Whatever sentence Judge John G. Koeltl hands down will be the first in the U.S. for AI-enabled streaming fraud. This type of criminal prosecution was also a first for the country. U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton has said, “the songs and the listeners were fake, but the millions of dollars Smith stole were real.”

Smith was first indicted in September 2024 on three counts: wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Prosecutors say he made the songs together with the unnamed CEO of an AI music company and a music promoter. According to the indictment, Smith calculated that bots could generate about 661,440 streams a day and $1,207,128 in annual royalties.

ABYZOR has added a free local AI module to Genesis, its MIDI-generation plugin for macOS and Windows. Genesis, released in June, is a plugin that creates melodies, basslines, chord progressions and arpeggios. You edit the results, then drag them into your DAW.
The new module does not replace the existing generator. It runs as an optional engine alongside Genesis v2.2.0, so the original procedural MIDI generation still works without the module.

Installing the module turns a single Genesis pattern into several versions. Transform mode keeps the original mood, Pitch Remix changes the notes while keeping the rhythm, and Keep Groove draws new material from the existing groove. You can run a whole pattern or pick specific bars, which is useful for growing ideas. The output is editable MIDI, so you can fix awkward notes and keep only the parts you like.

The engine runs locally on CPU or GPU and works offline once installed. There are no generation credits, API keys or subscription fees. ABYZOR said it plans to keep the module free going forward. The current beta uses the MIDI-GPT conversion pipeline, a symbolic music model aimed at bar-level infilling and controlled MIDI generation rather than finished audio.

If you don't have Genesis yet, you need to download two things. The email field on the Genesis download form is optional and can be left blank. The separate AI module installer is about 93MB for Windows and about 43MB for macOS. The installer then downloads the local engine from Hugging Face. According to ABYZOR's documentation, the engine package is roughly 400MB to 3GB, so the total size is far larger than the first installer file.

ABYZOR warns that this is still a public beta, so behavior and compatibility may change. Windows support covers 64-bit Windows 10 and 11. The macOS AI module is currently Apple Silicon only and unsigned, so you may need to click "Open Anyway" in Privacy & Security to launch it. Genesis ships as VST3 on Windows and VST3/AU on macOS. The AI module is not a plugin format; it's a separate local engine that runs on its own.
Suno posted a short clip showing Suno Studio. The caption is two lines: it says that recording your voice in Suno Studio can turn it into "anything," and that an electric guitar is "just the start."
In the video, the creator says he wants to add a short electric guitar moment between parts of the song, and suggests singing it in first. The hummed melody comes back as guitar sound.
A well-known Japanese actor and anime voice actor has filed a lawsuit against TikTok. The trigger was a series of videos suspected of using an AI-cloned version of his voice.

In Japan's anime industry, voice actors are sometimes loved as much as the characters they play. Kenjiro Tsuda, known for Jujutsu Kaisen and Yu-Gi-Oh!, is one such case. He may be the first Japanese voice actor to take a major company to court over alleged AI voice cloning. The video series in question carries narration that bears a striking resemblance to his voice; he is 55 this year.

According to court records, TikTok counters that the voice is just an "ordinary male voice," saying any resemblance to Tsuda's distinctive "glossy" baritone is subjective. But the anonymous account in question posted photos resembling a Jujutsu Kaisen character Tsuda voices.

The videos pair images with narration about urban legends and conspiracy theories; the narration is believed to be AI-generated. Tsuda's legal team estimates the account once had more than 200,000 subscribers and likely earned more than 500,000 yen (about $3,200) a month. The team argues the account "gained popularity only by reading suspicious, low-quality content in the appealing voice of a popular character."

Yuko Sasaki, managing director of the Japan Federation of Actors, said an actor's voice is "the result of years of harsh training and practice" and is "refined with a great deal of time and money." She added that courts "should recognize ownership of one's voice as a basic right," and that the union "fully supports" Tsuda.

TikTok challenges Tsuda's "nationwide fame" and recognition from the outset. It also denies that the account violated Japan's Unfair Competition Prevention Act by riding on an already-known brand. The company's position is that it merely provides "a space within the bounds of freedom of expression where users post creative and quirky content," seeking to play down its role in any infringement.

Tatsuhiro Ueno, a professor researching intellectual property at Waseda University, said the chance Tsuda would fail to be recognized as having a publicity right over his voice is "very low." He said his voice is "well known even in Europe" thanks to the ongoing popularity of Jujutsu Kaisen, and predicted the case would draw international attention as well.

blocks.cap: Waveforms of various instruments appear on screen while AI music is made with Suno. /Photo=Newsis

blocks.x: “It's rainy today, make me a soft ballad that fits the season.” One line of prompt is enough to produce a convincing song in seconds. That is the power of Suno, the generative AI music service with over 100 million subscribers. Foreign outlets such as The New York Times (NYT), Financial Times (FT), and The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) have each covered the ripple effects AI has had on the music industry and the shaken notion of 'authenticity'.

According to the FT, French streaming platform Deezer said more than half of the tracks newly uploaded last July, an average of 90,000 songs a month, were AI-generated. A bigger problem is 'streaming fraud,' in which tracks are mass-produced with AI and play counts are inflated with bots. Deezer said last year up to 85% of streams of 100% AI-generated tracks were fraudulent.

Major labels such as Sony, Universal, and Warner have sued Suno, alleging it trained on millions of copyrighted works without permission. Yet Warner Music and others are reportedly already investing in AI model development through licensing deals with Suno and Udio. The NYT described AI as, for the existing industry, “both a 'pirate' to be sued and a 'partner' to team up with for new revenue.”

The column calls for creator-protection systems to be quickly aligned with global standards. It warns that the moment the premium of a human artist's story and on-stage presence is lost, fans' wallets close too.
ElevenLabs released two new voice models on Monday, ElevenLabs v4 and v4 Turbo. They offer finer control over expression, cut latency for voice agents, and support more than 90 languages.

The company unveiled v3 last year and previewed this new model earlier this year at an event in Warsaw. The v4 generation uses a new architecture, giving tighter control and faster cloning. According to the company, just 10 seconds of audio is enough to clone a voice.

On the creative side, it holds onto a voice's identity better even across long text. It reads text aloud while adjusting expression based on the context of the writing. The company also expanded the inline expression tags introduced in v3; stacking multiple tags now lets the model follow their order.
Supported languages grew from 70 in the previous version to 90. The languages with the biggest quality gains were Japanese, Brazilian Portuguese, Mandarin and Cantonese.

ElevenLabs has rapidly grown its enterprise calling business over the past year. More than 55% of revenue now comes from large companies. The company says the new models have low enough latency for smooth conversation, making them well suited to voice agents. As soon as the LLM running behind the scenes starts generating an answer, audio generation begins, and situations like complaints, escalation to a supervisor, or being put on hold are handled differently, solving problems more effectively.

Competition among voice models has heated up. Startups like Cartesia, Deepgram, Fish Audio, Bosun and WellSaid Labs have released expressive voice models, and Google and OpenAI have also upgraded their voice models.

ElevenLabs raised $500 million from Sequoia earlier this year at a $11 billion valuation. Rumors are also circulating about a follow-on round at a $22 billion valuation. Annualized revenue jumped from about $330 million at the start of the year to more than $600 million. Aggressive hiring in India, Europe and Brazil has pushed headcount past 800. Co-founder and CEO Mati Staniszewski said in a recent TechCrunch interview that the company plans to go public "within the next few years," though he did not give a specific timeline.

blocks.cap: Todd Edwards

blocks.x: Todd Edwards, a house and UK garage legend and master of sampling, sat down for a long conversation with MusicRadar. He covered his 34-year career, his first UK show, his repeated collaborations with Daft Punk, and his thoughts on today's DJ culture.

His first piece of gear was an Ensoniq EPS sampling workstation. Its signature 13-bit grit and famous swing both came from there. With no keyboard at the time, he stitched together hundreds of short samples to build music and lyrics. He recalls that he "treated records like paint, like raw material."

With hundreds of micro samples in a single track, clearing each one individually is close to impossible. As AI made it easier to detect samples and copyright lawsuits grew more common, he had to change his approach. In early 2025 he tried playing synths or making his own samples with Splice, but he missed the joy of digging through records, and it left him depressed.

blocks.cap: Todd Edwards

blocks.x: The breakthrough was the AI music platform Suno Studio. Making material he could safely sample there brought back the joy of making music. "I hate it when people talk about this technology like it came from the devil," he says. He adds that seasoned producers see it as a powerful tool, while those without skills see it as a threat.

He believes making stems with AI to sample is no less creative than picking a Splice loop. That's also where he says "the hypocrisy in the industry is remarkable." A plain prompt alone produces something generic, he says, but if he puts in his own ideas to make a disco or soft rock track and then cuts it up, "it's all mine, so I never have to worry about a lawsuit again."
Having made music his whole life without AI, he says he uses it because "it's an amazing adventure," adding that in the end it comes down to how you use it.
Sampleson Backgrounds is a new soundscape-creation tool. Combining words and ideas on a canvas produces an ever-shifting, cinematic ambience.

At its core is semantic audio search, matching words and concepts against a curated library of over 22,000 audio cells and 11,000 local embeddings. Users build soundscapes by dragging keywords like strings, rain, bass, and thunder onto the canvas and blending them.
It runs entirely on your own computer, with no cloud processing or subscription tokens. It comes as a standalone app and a plugin, ready for use directly in music production and sound design work.
It is available now as a standalone app for macOS and Windows and as a VST3/AU plugin. The launch price is $39 (regular price $59).

blocks.cap: IMPF/IMPEL AI licensing principles

blocks.x: IMPF and IMPEL, representing independent music publishers, have put out principles the industry should follow when licensing to generative AI platforms. At the top is one "non-negotiable" principle: songs must be properly valued, and unless there is some other clear reason, they must be paid at least as much as recordings.

When AI companies use existing music for training and services, this calls for pricing the royalties for the two rights embedded in a single track — the recording (master) right and the song (composition) right — at nearly the same level. In streaming, recordings have always been paid far more than songs. The two groups say that, having disputed streaming's imbalance for years, they see generative AI as a chance to build a fairer framework, and that a model which gives songs a small share while directing most of the revenue to masters is "unacceptable."

They stress that songs, lyrics, and melodies sit at the center of AI music products, from training through prompting, generation, output, and commercialization. They also said licensing scope must be specific and must not inadvertently create a pathway to broader future uses.

They also called for transparency. Rights holders should know what is being licensed, how works are used and how attribution is handled, what deductions apply, and how revenue is calculated and distributed. Payments for past use, training, output, and future use should be clearly separated and treated fairly.

As majors push their AI partners to prioritize remix and mashup tools that use existing tracks, at least two separate revenue streams arise: payment for training and payment for use of output. Since the two streams may be split differently, the principles become more useful. IMPF chair Annette Barrett said, "Songs are at the heart of all of this and must be protected."

blocks.cap: Anthology

blocks.x: UK-based Absolute Label Services is opening its AI-driven music operating system, Anthology, to the entire independent music industry. It's a white-label business management platform, and its first customers are Cherry Red Records and Blue Raincoat Music, part of Reservoir Media.

At Absolute, a "music OS" isn't a single feature—it's the company's term for software that spans a rights company's data and operations as a whole. Anthology links together global digital and physical distribution, neighboring-rights registration, marketing, financial reporting, inventory and supplier management, and invoicing. Running through all of it is Absolute's own LLM, "Ant."

Simon Wills, who leads Anthology, said concerns about "what AI means for creativity, copyright and the value of human-made music are legitimate," but added that "AI is much bigger than generating music." He said the focus was on helping people rather than replacing them—letting AI watch over data around the clock to catch anomalies, royalty issues and business opportunities that are easy to miss.

He explained that Ant is rooted in decades of music-industry knowledge built up by Absolute, and that customers retain full data sovereignty. The company spent several years and several million pounds building the system, and has been using it internally since July 2024.

Cherry Red's Matt Bristow said he's had to enter data separately into 15 platforms for a single release, and that with around 30 releases a month, the system will save significant time every month. Wills said music companies can't keep negotiating with the likes of Google, Apple, Meta and Spotify using PDFs and spreadsheets, and stressed that music companies need their own technological capability.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit upheld a lower-court ruling that AI companies' copying of copyrighted works to build training data is not fair use. The court sided with Thomson Reuters, which owns the legal search service Westlaw. Its opponent was Ross Intelligence, a startup that built a competing search tool using Westlaw's case summaries (headnotes) and has since shut down.

The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and the National Music Publishers' Association (NMPA) filed a joint brief arguing that training AI models on copyrighted works to build a competing service "cannot be fair use." The 32-page ruling remains under seal. Once unsealed, it will become binding precedent for district courts in the circuit.

The two groups cited a filing in which Suno said it trained its model on "nearly all of the quality music files available on the internet." They also cited figures Deezer disclosed showing it was receiving more than 50,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day in November 2025, a number that grew to nearly 90,000 a day by June of this year. They pointed to deals between UMG and Warner with Stability AI and Udio, and between Kobalt and ElevenLabs, as evidence that a real market for training-data licensing exists.

Still, the ruling doesn't resolve the fair-use question in the Suno and Udio cases. Ross was a tool for finding existing case law, not generative AI. Judge Stephanos Bibas, who issued the lower-court ruling, drew that same line in his 2025 decision, writing that it dealt "only with non-generative AI." Suno and Udio are building their defenses around fair use. In the Massachusetts case against Suno, both sides plan to file for summary judgment on fair use.

This is a conversation Thomas Bangalter had with Yana Peel, CHANEL's global head of arts, culture and heritage, at Art Basel. When AI came up, he said flatly that he has little interest in using artificial intelligence for creation.

This is an op-ed Andreea Gleeson, former CEO of TuneCore, wrote for Music Business Worldwide. It starts from the diagnosis that the AI situation has already moved into commercialization, while the industry is still fumbling to catch up with the rules.

The evidence she cites: more than 90,000 AI tracks are uploaded to Deezer every day, passing half of all new uploads, and TIDAL has decided to exclude fully AI-made recordings from royalties. IFPI has put out chart-eligibility principles, and Spotify and Universal Music Group have opened licensed AI tools. The market is writing the rules before legislation catches up.
It's not an unfamiliar picture. In 2007 with YouTube's Content ID, and in 2008 with Spotify, market standards also arrived ahead of regulation. AI is following the same track.

According to a Luminate survey, 54% of U.S. musicians were positive about AI tools, versus 35% of non-musician respondents. On the other side, 46% of listeners showed resistance to AI voices making entirely new songs. That reads as listeners also drawing a line between AI that assists human creation and AI that replaces it.
Gleeson divides AI music into four layers: creation, distribution, attribution and consumption. The information captured upstream directly shapes the outcomes downstream.
As examples of participation rather than replacement, she cites the licensed AI-voice collaboration with Robert Owens, and the Spotify-Merlin partnership that legally clears fan-made remixes.

Her core argument is that detection is the wrong fight. Rather than trying to guess the recipe after dinner is already plated, the idea is to keep a record the moment the ingredients go in. As with organic certification, reliable metadata should be attached at the moment the DAW creates it.
Once AI labels start determining royalty splits and chart eligibility, metadata becomes money. Standardizing the label alone isn't enough; verifiable provenance has to follow from upstream.

So Gleeson redefines this as an interoperability problem rather than a copyright one. Work on MIDI 2.0 shows a way to pass provenance back and forth across a song's entire lifecycle, and movements like the Music Tech Coalition, which involves Peter Brown and Venable, are stitching scattered efforts into a single commercial infrastructure. What's needed now isn't new technology, but coordination.

blocks.cap: Reflector — an open source sample-browsing workstation that scans libraries by harmonic relationships

blocks.x: Austin Rockman, a composer and software engineer, has released Reflector, a free open source sample-browsing workstation.

Machine learning finds its way into just about every music tool these days. What makes this one stand out is that it's less about stamping out more sounds and more about letting you work with audio differently.

It's simple to use. You point it at a folder of sounds, it analyzes them on-device, and from there it finds sounds that pair well with a given sample or that sound similar. It browses your library by harmonic relationship rather than by folder name.
If you like one sample, it points you toward other sounds that could lock in with it harmonically. If a pitch shift would make something fit better, it even suggests the transposition.
It doesn't stop at a single search either. Lay samples out roughly on a DAW-like timeline, and it watches what's happening in the current session to offer its next suggestion.

Austin calls this a pre-DAW stage. It isn't meant to replace your main music software. It's a place to throw sounds around, see what fits, and then pull out WAVs or stems to continue the work elsewhere.

Right now it targets material with harmonic content, like pads, keys, strings, synths, guitar, vocals, and pitch-centered field recordings. It doesn't analyze rhythm, so it isn't a beat-matching tool.

There's also a Galaxy view that scatters your saved sessions across a 3D space, showing which arrangements connect harmonically. If you have a large library or a pile of unfinished sketches, this is where you might rediscover connections you'd forgotten about.

All processing runs on-device, and neither audio nor usage history leaves your machine. The model was trained only on synthetic audio rather than copyrighted recordings. Austin has made clear that the weights, model code and training pipeline are all open source, and that it will stay free going forward.
As experimental software from a solo developer, expect some rough edges. Right now it's available as a signed macOS application.

Two class-action lawsuits have been filed accusing Suno of storing user data in a manner that was “negligent and/or reckless.” The plaintiffs claim the company knew about the security risk and did nothing about it.

The suits were filed by Suno users Frank Rugnetta and Alec Pilavian. Both filed in Massachusetts, where Suno is headquartered, and are seeking class-action status representing all affected U.S. users.

The breach happened in November 2025 and came to light only recently through reporting by 404 Media. The accessed information covered 55.3 million Suno users and included names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, purchase history and some payment card information.
The leaked data also included Suno's source code. That revealed that the company had scraped songs and lyrics from Deezer, Genius and YouTube to use for AI training.
Suno never formally notified users of the breach. It acknowledged the security incident only after the reporting came out.

The causes of action in the lawsuits are negligence, breach of implied contract, breach of good faith, and unjust enrichment. The plaintiffs say they now face a lifetime risk of fraud, identity theft and invasion of privacy.

blocks.cap: Saregama — India's oldest record label is adding AI video to its catalog

blocks.x: Saregama, India's oldest record label, founded around 1901, is making AI-generated music videos for 1960s–70s film songs using generative AI. The label, part of the RP-Sanjiv Goenka Group, holds the recording and composition rights but not the rights to the original footage. CEO Vikram Mehra revealed the effort during the company's fiscal Q1 earnings call on August 4. Saregama Music's YouTube channel has about 64 million subscribers.

The reason there's no footage is simple. Back when the films were made, there was no market for selling the footage to labels, so it stayed locked inside the film negatives held by the movie studios. It's a burden that newer rival labels don't carry. Shooting new footage never made financial sense before, but AI has driven the cost down. Mehra said it "can be INR 70,000 also" — about 70,000 rupees, or roughly $740.

There are two target generations. For Gen X, the original audio stays untouched while new, modern-feeling visuals are added. For Gen Z, the composition is left alone but the arrangement gets reworked before being paired with new AI video.

The second track using generative AI is this: third-party tools create podcast-like audio, laid over music from the company's own catalog. A fifty-year-old narrator reminisces while following along to songs about love, breakups, and friendship. There are also plans to license this out to other podcast producers.

Mehra split AI into two tracks. Predictive AI, which has been running for four years and is used to decide on acquiring rights, now has a better hit-to-miss ratio, he said. Generative AI, he said, is the one that changes the game entirely. The content-acquisition budget runs 300–350 crore rupees a year, or $31.6 million to $36.9 million.

He also restated the company's position on rights. It supports licensed innovation and opposes unauthorized use. New digital licensing deals now include clauses against rights dilution and fraud. Back in May, Mehra said streaming services should value AI-generated music at zero.

The film business is being wound down. Instead, in December 2025, the company put in $36 million to buy a stake in Bhansali Productions and secure exclusive rights to its upcoming film music. For Gen Z, it connects through Pocket Aces and its FilterCopy studio, fully acquired in 2024 for $45 million.

The catalog runs to about 180,000 songs and grows by 5,000 a year. In fiscal year 2026, 60% of music revenue came from songs released after 2000, and 45% from songs after 2020. Older songs are monetized directly through Carvaan, the company's retro player and streaming app. The in-house AI team has built two new units, one for content and one for process, running within the existing budget with no extra spending.

Fiscal Q1 revenue was 263.6 crore rupees, or $27.8 million, up 27% year over year. Adjusted EBITDA jumped 69% to 112.4 crore rupees, or $11.8 million. The music segment alone grew 39% to 230.6 crore rupees, or $24.3 million.

Mehra sees India's paid subscribers reaching 100 million, on the assumption that free music shrinks and prices rise toward around 100 rupees a month. Paid streaming today accounts for just 3% of India's internet users, according to Goldman Sachs. In 2025 alone, India added nearly 4 million paid subscriptions, bringing the cumulative total to 14.4 million.

blocks.x: In an August 7 release note, Suno said its vocal cloning feature, Voices, now works on iOS and Android. The feature launched in March alongside the v5.5 model, but until now it had to be set up on desktop.

There are three ways to use it: record yourself singing, upload an audio file, or pick a track from your own Suno library. The platform isolates the vocal used for training on its own, and verifies that the voice is really yours by having you read a confirmation phrase out loud.

Free users now also get a limited taste of Voices. Using it further requires an upgrade. Pro and Premier subscribers remain unlimited as before. Voices created are private by default, so only the account owner can use them.

This also caps off a run of recent updates. iMessage integration, CarPlay and Android Auto support, and improved stem-separation tools all arrived in succession. A waitlist has also opened for Suno Vinyl, which presses AI-made songs onto physical records. Pricing is set at around $45, shipping not included.

Around the same time, Suno said it's adding audio watermarking and fingerprinting. The goal is to catch fraud happening on streaming platforms, and it has also set a new download policy meant to block mass distribution.

Copyright disputes remain tangled on multiple fronts. In July, a German court found infringement in the GEMA case, and Denmark's Koda has a separate claim. In the U.S., Universal Music Group and Sony Music are suing, with claims that could exceed $9 billion.

blocks.cap: Machine Unlearning Research Hub — a library on whether training data can really be erased

blocks.x: AI developers offer skeptical musicians one safety valve: if you don't like how your music is being used, they'll remove it later. Chris Castle of MusicTechPolicy thinks that promise is close to fiction in practice.

Removing a single song from an already-trained neural network is, as The Trichordist puts it, like trying to take the eggs back out of a baked cake. The moment a model learns a track, trillions of internal values shift across the entire system.

Castle put it this way: "Creators should not assume that a contractual promise to 'remove' works from future training is equivalent to proving that an existing model has actually forgotten them." A contractual promise to exclude a work from future training is a different thing from proving that an already-built model has actually forgotten it.
He opened the Machine Unlearning Research Hub to close this gap between what the technology claims and what it actually does.

The hub is a public library collecting peer-reviewed papers on machine unlearning along with audio research and policy analysis. Machine unlearning refers to a still-theoretical procedure for making a system forget specific training data without rebuilding it from scratch.

Musicians have four uses for it. If an AI startup claims it can easily opt artists out or delete catalogs even after training, the hub's research can be used to check that claim. By showing that retroactive deletion isn't currently possible, it pins down for platforms why upfront consent and licensing fees are necessary.

It also tracks real progress in audio unlearning, such as post-hoc pruning or output filters, serving as a window to watch for whether true data deletion ever becomes possible. And when someone argues that unauthorized scraping can simply be papered over with unlearning later, it serves as grounds to push back in copyright debates.

Hypebot's conclusion is short: when you sit down with an AI music company, don't trade upfront permission or payment for a promise to delete things later. Until real machine unlearning is possible, strict consent obtained before training is the only real protection.
Build artists' rights on solid science, so musicians don't end up buying a fake delete button. That's the goal Chris Castle and the new hub have set.

Mastering The Mix has released a new immersive EQ plugin, MIXVAULT, for macOS and Windows.

blocks.cap: MIXVAULT — an EQ interface that lets you push and pull sound in a 3D room

blocks.x: It follows REFERENCE 3 and STEREOVAULT. Think of it as a ground-up overhaul of the company's earlier EQ tools, MIXROOM and BASSROOM.

The idea is simple: treat EQ not as curve editing, but as handling the sound right in front of you. Instead of dragging nodes up and down, you pull a given frequency forward to bring it out, or push it back to tuck it away.

The interface is a 3D room view that responds as you work. A hertz strip on the wall lets you zoom into the band you want. Fine control still remains: scroll over a band to change the Q, or double-click a dB value to type in a number directly.

A lot of effort went into honest monitoring. MIXVAULT level-matches every adjustment in real time, so instead of the illusion that something sounds better just because it's louder, you hear the actual tonal change. It also comes with a live delta display showing how the EQ is altering the signal, and a Delta button that lets you toggle between the dry and processed sound.

It also analyzes the audio to build Smart Presets suited to the source and genre. Pick from mix, vocal, drums, bass, or music, and you can step through tonal directions one notch at a time, from dark and thick to bright and forward. These aren't fixed curves being loaded in — they're presets pulled from that specific audio right now.

There are four resolution modes. Broad uses four wide bands to shape tone quickly, and Balanced handles general mastering with six bands. Detailed digs into problem spots with nine narrow bands, and Bass concentrates five bands between 20Hz and 320Hz.

The Bass mode is an improved version of the BASSROOM filter, shaping low end while minimizing phase and transient distortion. The company says MIXVAULT's default filter matches the frequency response of the top setting on the market's leading linear-phase EQ, while running at 36 times lower latency.

You can also load a reference track as a tonal target and compare it with levels matched. It also comes with A/B states, undo and redo, full bypass, trim, a dry/wet mix, keyboard shortcuts, and a resizable interface.

It's priced at $80 / £59 / €70.95, with a 15-day free trial. The launch discount runs through September 4, 2026, giving both new and existing customers 30% off, with an added loyalty discount for existing users. Owners of MIXROOM and BASSROOM get 50% off.
Formats are VST3, AU, and AAX. macOS supports both Intel and Apple Silicon on 10.15 or later, and it runs on Windows 10 or later.

For almost thirty years, my songs lived only in a notebook. I finished writing the lyrics, but the melodies always came to me only in fragments, I didn't know how to play an instrument, and there was no one to hand the lyrics to.

blocks.cap: Hypebot op-ed — a record from singer-songwriter Jeff Kaiser, who turned 30 years of lyrics into songs

blocks.x: Then I found Suno. I barely knew anything about prompts, only the sound I wanted: a warm male vocal, acoustic guitar, an unhurried tempo, honest country. The first attempt was this simple: “Country song. Male singer. Acoustic guitar. Slow tempo.”
I pasted in the lyrics and hit Generate. A minute later, my song was coming out of the speakers. Even now, with twenty-six songs made, that feeling hasn't worn off.
Even a basic prompt can produce something convincing. With Suno, the hard part isn't writing — it's aiming. The first two songs I picked from the notebook went through dozens of runs.

I had to build up the skill of putting the sound in my head into words first. So I talked it through with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok, explaining what I wanted, then showed each one what the others came up with to push further. For nine months, that was the whole method.

Then I came across a seven-page guide someone had posted for free. It wasn't about music — it was about Suno. Prompts have a character limit, and earlier words carry more weight. Each word has to narrow something down, and whatever you don't want goes to the very end. Half the work isn't the prompt at all — it's the tags planted inside the lyrics.

“She Came Out of the Blue,” out September 4, is the first song where I applied that method all the way through. The mood is a late-night, cinematic Gulf Coast air; the vocal is a weathered country baritone; the production is analog warmth with “No glossy pop sheen. No organ.” Unlike the other songs I ran dozens of times, this one came out the way I wanted on the first pass.

Once two songs became twenty-six in a year, I wondered what would happen if I handed them to musicians. Making that first contact was harder than prompting. I put together a glossary of music terms, called and emailed Nashville demo studios directly, and found the rest through AirGigs and SoundBetter. My worry turned out to be misplaced. No one treated me like a joke.

On “Winding On,” out February 5, producer Vito Astone rebuilt every instrumental part from scratch and added a fingerpicked acoustic intro. Abbie Parker sang lead. On the line “Some things break and just stay broken,” her voice caught, just barely. Those were lyrics I'd been carrying for years.
Since November 2025 I've released one song a month, and cumulative streams are approaching 200,000. One track was used in Florida tourism promotion. But that's not the point.

AI didn't write the lyrics. It made the music, and it took a year to learn how to aim it. What I couldn't do for 30 years wasn't writing — it was finishing. The software didn't replace Vito or Abbie. It just introduced us.

blocks.cap: Beatport's AI music ban (Photo courtesy of Beatport)

blocks.x: Beatport has started filtering out AI-made music. The dance music download store has added Beatdapp's detection tool to its catalog, a system meant to catch tracks that are entirely or mostly AI-made at the point of upload.
The AI policy itself has been in place since January 2025. What's new is the technology actually enforcing it. How well the tool catches things remains to be seen over the coming months.

Music made entirely by AI is held during ingestion, and the rights holder is notified right away. AI-assisted work is treated differently. “Music made with AI assistance will continue to be accepted as long as the finished track is predominantly human-made,” Beatport's policy page states. Such releases get flagged at the import stage, so the curation team knows what it's looking at during review.
Beatdapp was originally a partner for streaming fraud detection. With this new AI detection tool, that collaboration has expanded into music identification as well.

Beatport says the decision directly reflects where the community stands. In a user survey, 60% said they would not play AI-generated tracks in their sets, and 77% made clear they would support human creators. 8% said they were open to playing AI music, while 13% said they'd consider it if fair compensation went to artists and labels.

Beatport CEO Matt Gralen summed it up this way: “Beatport exists for DJs, and to empower artists and labels. New production techniques have pushed electronic music forward from the start, but tools that help human creativity are different from systems that replace creativity altogether. Beatport was built on the former.”

Beatdapp co-founder and co-CEO Andrew Batey noted that the music industry has always embraced new technology, adding that what's needed now is infrastructure that brings real transparency to the generative AI era. AFEM Chief Strategy Officer Jay Ahern said this approach aligns with AFEM's AI principles: human intent and creative control should sit alongside consent, licensing, transparency, provenance labeling, and fair compensation.

The timing isn't a coincidence. Last month, Paris-based streaming giant Deezer confirmed that about 50% of its platform's daily uploads — roughly 90,000 tracks — are AI-generated. In early August, Spotify said it would add an 'AI Persona' badge to AI-generated artist profiles. In June, reporting by The Atlantic revealed that AI developers had used about 21 million copyrighted tracks to train their models.

Pairing a full ban on AI music with automated detection is a consistent choice for a DJ-focused platform. It won't work perfectly for a while. Untouched AI music is caught relatively well, but once it's edited, layered with human vocals, and mixed with other sounds, even sophisticated tools struggle to tell the difference. Still, that's better than having no rules at all, Gearnews concludes.

blocks.cap: IA De-Esser — a free de-esser with four slots

blocks.x: Immanent Audio has released IA De-Esser, a free de-essing and resonance-suppression plugin for macOS and Windows.

IA De-Esser takes a slightly different approach. Instead of a single module, it uses four filter slots to tame sibilance, harshness, and spiking resonance. Each slot can run as a De-Ess mode that reacts automatically to sibilance, or as a mode that handles a broader range of harsh sound.
It's a reasonable idea. Shaving off a little harshness in each module produces a more natural result than pushing a single de-esser hard.

In Auto mode, you just set the Low-Cut and Hi-Cut range, and the plugin picks the depth and Q values it judges appropriate. Smart mode goes a step further, scanning the spectrum and sending active slots to the points that need attention.

The goal is to trim away only the harshness you want gone, without letting the whole vocal or instrument collapse into that muffled, over-de-essed sound. The screen displays attack, release, depth, and Q in real time, so you can read what the plugin is doing.
It doesn't add to DAW latency, so it can just be left on even in situations like tracking, where delay is a problem.

With AI-made audio tools multiplying lately, we asked Immanent Audio whether this plugin was built with AI too. Developer Jay confirmed it, saying “AI was used to speed up the process.” He added that, as a software engineer by trade, he doesn't ship code he doesn't understand.
IA De-Esser is available free on Gumroad. It supports VST3 and AU formats on macOS and Windows.

blocks.cap: Spotify AI Persona · Source: Spotify

blocks.x: Spotify is introducing a new tag, the AI Persona label, for artist profiles that don't stand in for a real person. Starting mid-September 2026, these profiles will be marked on banners, in search, and on tracks within playlists. At the same time, Spotify will exclude these profiles from editorial and algorithmic recommendations by default.

Spotify says listener feedback was clear: people want to know whether a real person is behind a profile or an AI-made persona. Artists and their teams will now self-report whether their profile is an AI Persona. Spotify will also actively review profiles, including those using realistic AI-generated images. Within a few months, listeners will be able to flag profiles they suspect are unlabeled AI Personas. Spotify makes the final call.

The timing isn't a coincidence. The platform has been swamped with AI-made content for months. In April, Spotify already launched 'Verified by Spotify' to mark genuine artist profiles. The AI Persona label is part of a larger plan called 'Artist Identity & Trust,' which also includes SongDNA and AI song credits — tools for disclosing how an artist used AI in making music.

What really matters isn't the label itself, but what comes attached to it. Music from AI Persona profiles won't appear by default in either editorial or personalized recommendations. On a platform where music discovery runs largely on algorithmic playlists, that's close to blocking reach — even though Spotify officially describes it as just a label.

Payouts, however, stay the same. Royalties for AI Persona tracks are paid out as usual. What Spotify is targeting is exposure, not money. TIDAL went the opposite way in July, keeping AI tracks in its catalog but cutting them off entirely from royalties and direct sales.

In July, major industry bodies like IFPI and RIAA agreed on two voluntary labels, 'AI-Generated' and 'AI-Assisted.' The big streaming platforms didn't take part. Spotify, lukewarm at the time, has now chosen a different path. Where the industry bodies' labels mark how much AI went into a recording, Spotify's AI Persona label asks whether there's a person behind the profile at all.
Whether the label actually slows AI personas from crowding out real artists, or savvy operators simply find a way around it, won't be clear until after it takes effect in mid-September.

blocks.cap: A diagram of the IK Multimedia Tonex ecosystem

blocks.x: IK Multimedia has reworked Tonex Player from top to bottom. It now has a “photorealistic” gear selection screen and a streamlined workflow, and the public beta arrives together with 220 new Premium Tone Models.

Tonex 2.0 Player functions more like a creative hub within IK Multimedia's electric guitar and bass tone ecosystem. Managing Tone Models, edits, presets, and captures, and discovering new sounds, are all brought together in one place.
Sounds made here carry over directly to the entire lineup of Tonex hardware devices.
When IK Multimedia says the Tonex ecosystem is growing, that's not an exaggeration. The diagram with Tonex 2.0 Player sitting at the center of multiple hardware units gets more complex by the day.

Tonex 2.0 Player runs both as a guitar plugin and as a standalone app for your DAW. The moment you open it, you can see the home screen has changed. Gear, signal chains, and the library all open from here.

IK Multimedia explains it this way: “It's faster to find the sound you want, easier to shape it, and more rewarding to explore.” In other words, you find the sound you want faster, shape it more easily, and have more fun digging around.

The screen for browsing amp models now looks better. The connection to the ToneNET community has also tightened up, and the new Smart Search makes it easier to find user-made Tone Models and signal chain presets. A dedicated, resizable floating browser moves between amps, effects, and the Tonex collection.

This is the core of the Tonex model. The Tonex lineup, software and hardware alike, is designed to interlock completely with IK Multimedia's Amplitube 5 platform. What this overhaul is pushing for is a single workflow running from capture through studio, rehearsal, and stage.
Tonex 2.0 Player is open now as a public beta. It will soon roll out to all Tonex users as a free update.

blocks.cap: D'Addario — the subject of the controversial NYXL HD demo video

blocks.x: D'Addario admitted it used generative AI in a demo video for its NYXL HD extended-range electric guitar strings. The New York–based strings and accessories brand confirmed that Suno Studio was used to regenerate the original track.

The Instagram statement begins: "We got this wrong. We've completed a full review and confirmed that Suno Studio was used to regenerate the original track. We shared inaccurate information, and we're truly sorry."

Until then, the company had denied using AI, even releasing a video showing DAW stem files. YouTubers were the ones who dug into that claim. Danny Sapko raised the first questions, and scrutiny spread around a heavily processed progressive metal performance demo. Rhett Shull obtained the stem files directly and looked further into the controversy.
D'Addario artists like Yvette Young and Mike Dawes initially defended the brand. Things escalated after the company deleted critical comments and one employee claimed to have been doxxed.

In the statement, D'Addario said it had also mishandled comment moderation. "Honest criticism should not be erased." It added that it would change how it runs its channels so people are protected from threats, harassment, and doxxing while still being heard.

It also laid out a new policy. "We do not support AI-generated music, and our process will reflect that going forward." Employees and creative partners will now be required to disclose whether generative AI was used in content, and the company will review that disclosure closely.

It closed by saying it knows one statement won't fix this, that D'Addario exists because musicians have entrusted their sound to its products, and that it will earn the same trust in how it treats this community.

blocks.cap: Noizefield Audio Plugin Coder

blocks.x: Music software maker Noizefield has released Audio Plugin Coder (APC) 1.4.0, a major update to the open-source framework that uses AI coding agents to turn plugin ideas written in natural language into VST3/AU project structures.

APC guides users through ideation, architecture design, UI design, implementation, testing, and packaging, while carrying forward project state and troubleshooting knowledge throughout. It's aimed at producers, sound designers, and developers who don't want to start from an empty C++ project. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux alongside agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Kilo, and Antigravity.

Here's what's new in 1.4.0. It upgrades from JUCE 8 to JUCE 9.0.1, picking up support for the latest hosts, tooling, and WebView-based UI. /apc-setup is a first-run wizard that checks the toolchain and sets plugin, build, and release folder locations, UI defaults, and per-step AI model preferences.

Workflow commands also got unique names, like /apc-dream, /apc-plan, /apc-design, /apc-impl, and /apc-ship — a change meant to avoid name collisions with other AI tools, though short aliases like /dream still remain. Dependency checking has gotten tighter, and the WebView plugin documentation has improved. Build scripts were fixed to recognize paths correctly, and WebView UI smoke tests on Windows were verified against actual plugin builds.
APC 1.4.0 is available for free on GitHub, with the source code open as well.

blocks.cap: The transparency provision of the EU AI Act, in force since August 2

blocks.x: Since August 2, new transparency provisions under the European Union's AI Act have taken effect. Audio, images, video and text that AI created or substantially altered must now clearly disclose that they are “artificial”.
Developers of general-purpose AI systems now face new transparency obligations as well. It marks the first milestone consumers can actually feel in the EU's flagship AI legislation.
For the music industry, the change isn't about blocking AI but about making its use visible. It doesn't ban AI music, nor does it settle the copyright disputes over AI training data.

Instead, “the focus is on transparency”. Content that AI created or substantially altered must be recognizable to listeners, and developers must document how they trained their models and meet the AI Act's transparency requirements.

The music industry's biggest legal questions remain unanswered. The new rules don't determine whether companies like Suno or Udio infringed copyright by training on copyrighted recordings, nor do they require disclosing every song used in training. That fight continues in courtrooms and licensing negotiations around the world.
What Europe has set is a single baseline: “AI-made content can no longer be anonymous”.

For artists, labels and rights holders, it becomes easier to identify AI-generated output and examine how it is presented to listeners. Holding companies accountable for how they used AI also gets easier. Companies that violate the transparency requirements can face fines of up to €15 million, or 3% of their annual global revenue.

blocks.cap: The Spotify and Kobalt logos on a black background

blocks.x: Spotify has been teasing an AI tool that lets fans make covers and remixes for a while now. It has already disclosed a partnership with Universal Music Group. The new partner is indie music publisher Kobalt, a company that publishes songs for a wide range of musicians, from Phoebe Bridgers to post-punk band IDLES.

Kobalt artists will soon be able to opt into Spotify's new platform, where fans take songs and rework them into remixes and covers, powered, of course, by a suite of AI tools. No one has heard the results yet. Think something like Suno, but using only properly licensed songs instead of scraping the whole internet.

So the tool is being promoted not as a new way for generative AI to rip off artists, but as a new way for them to make money. Spotify says it will “open up additional revenue streams and new ways to drive discovery”. Kobalt CEO Laurent Hubert added that its artists are “directly benefiting from the creative opportunities these new features provide”.

At least it's clear where that revenue will come from. The platform will launch as a paid add-on for Premium subscribers. It's still unknown how much it will cost, or whether anyone will actually pay to make an AI cover of a favorite song.

It's also unclear whether there will be a way to make covers without AI. If it really all comes down to licensing, what's the difference between algorithmic slop and a real cover performed and recorded by a human? Either way, answers will take a while to arrive. Spotify hasn't said when the tool will launch.

blocks.cap: Suno co-founder and CEO Mikey Shulman. Photo by Samuel Boivin / Shutterstock
